name: Waldtraut vom Mühlwald

location.address: Mühlwald, Günterstäler Stadtwald (city forest), Freiburg im Breisgau

access: Free, in the public city forest (Stadtwald). No ticket, no gate; reached by a signed forest trail.
transport: Line 21 (bus) to the 'Kyburg' stop in Günterstal, then a signed 2.5 km forest hike (about 150 m of ascent) along the Mühlwaldweg following 'Höchster Baum Deutschlands' signs; or a 4.5 km hike from Waldhaus Freiburg at Wonnhalde. Not a quick stop, a proper forest walk of an hour or more each way from the tram network.
story:
The tallest tree in Germany is not a German species and it is only 116 years old. Waldtraut vom Mühlwald is a coastal Douglas fir, planted in 1913 as a three-year-old sapling in a forestry trial that had been putting North American conifers into the Freiburg city forest since 1896. The age comes from a written planting date rather than a guess. The height, measured in April 2024, is 67.85 metres.

It is still going up. Five years earlier it was measured at 67.10 metres, and the two sources that track it differ slightly on the current rate, somewhere between 15 and 30 centimetres a year. Both call it vigorous. The trunk is 3.38 metres round at chest height, which for that height is slender. Freiburg's own foresters gave it the name.

The experiment it belongs to is still standing around it: several more Douglas firs of the same 1913 planting, none of which won the title. A century-old test of whether an American conifer would take in the hills above Freiburg, with the answer visible from a long way off.

Be realistic about getting there. It is a signed forest walk of about 2.5 kilometres from the Kyburg stop in Günterstal, roughly 150 metres of climb, an hour or more each way. There is no viewing platform. There are wooden information boards at the foot of the tree, and a lot of looking straight up.

name: The Sedanquartier Weeping Beech

location.address: Corner of Wilhelmstraße and Moltkestraße, Sedanquartier, Freiburg im Breisgau

access: Free, on a publicly reachable plot at a street corner. Stands on land owned by the State of Baden-Württemberg (Landesgrund) rather than a private owner, beside the public sculpture 'Kaichina Doll' by Peter Zimmermann; a city celebration for the designation was held right at the tree in November 2021.
transport: In the Sedanquartier, roughly 1 km south of the Altstadt centre; reachable on foot or by tram/bus to a Wiehre-area stop.
story:
The State of Baden-Württemberg owned the plot, wanted to build on it, and lost to the tree. This weeping beech stands on the corner of Wilhelmstraße and Moltkestraße on state-owned land in the Sedanquartier, and in 2020 a member of the state parliament, Gabi Rolland, filed a formal question pressing for its protection. The government's answer acknowledged the tree's ecological value and noted, in the same breath, that the plot's development value was considerable too.

The tree won. Freiburg designated it a natural monument on 29 October 2021, one of thirty announced together, which took the city's total to 130. A week later the neighbourhood's residents' group held a small ceremony at the trunk with the environment mayor present. Very few trees anywhere get a party.

The press covering the row never called it anything more precise than a splendid deciduous tree and a giant, which is the useful part of the record and also its limit. Nobody has measured its girth or dated it, and no source names the cultivar; it is almost certainly the standard weeping form of the European beech, but that is a reasonable assumption rather than a documented one. If you can tell us how thick it is, we will put the number on this page.

It shares its corner with a public sculpture, the Kaichina Doll by Peter Zimmermann, so the walk gives you two things to stand in front of.

name: The Bernhardstraße Ginkgo

location.address: Bernhardstraße, near the corner with Habsburgerstraße, Freiburg im Breisgau

access: Free, a street tree on a former parking lot in an ordinary residential and commercial street; freely visible and reachable, no gate or ticket.
transport: Central Freiburg, on Bernhardstraße near Habsburgerstraße, easy walking distance of the Altstadt.
story:
The car park is gone and the ginkgo is protected. This gnarled, fan-crowned tree stands on a former parking lot on Bernhardstraße towards Habsburgerstraße, in a perfectly ordinary stretch of shops and flats, and Freiburg's council made it a natural monument on 28 January 2011, in a batch of ten. The local report on that decision called it markant and knorrig, striking and gnarled, and singled out the golden autumn foliage as something the street watches for.

Ginkgo biloba is the last survivor of an order of trees that was widespread when dinosaurs were, and the fossil leaves are close enough to the living ones that you can match them by eye. It is also one of the toughest trees a European city can plant, largely indifferent to exhaust fumes, road salt and compacted ground, which is why so many end up on pavements and, evidently, car parks.

Nobody has recorded when this one was planted or how thick it is. That is a genuine gap rather than a hedge, and it is the sort of thing a person with a tape measure could close in a minute. If that is you, tell us.

One warning for cross-checkers: Freiburg has at least three registered ginkgos, so go by the street rather than the species. This is the Bernhardstraße one.

best_time.label: November, when the leaves turn gold and then drop almost all at once

name: The Alexandereiche

location.address: Corner of Einsteinstraße and Hermann-Mitsch-Straße, Freiburg im Breisgau

access: Free, an ordinary street-corner tree, not on any private or institutional grounds mentioned in either source.
transport: Northern Freiburg, roughly 3.9 km from the Altstadt centre; a separate outing rather than part of a single Altstadt walk, reachable by tram/bus.
story:
The Alexandereiche is not named after Alexander von Humboldt, which is the first thing almost everyone assumes. Freiburg's own environment office says the oak carries the name of Alexander Wasmer, the city's chief forester, who drew up the first management plan for the Freiburg city forest in 1842. A forester's paperwork is a thin sort of immortality, and a street-corner oak is more than most of them get.

Note what that does not tell us. The city names the tree for what Wasmer did in 1842; no source anywhere says the tree was planted then, or gives it an age at all, and we are not going to turn a commemoration into a birth date. Nobody has published a girth for it either. Even the species is only recorded as oak: the register does not say whether it is a pedunculate or a sessile oak, and the two are easy to tell apart on the ground, since one hangs its acorns on stalks and the other sits them tight against the twig. If you go and look, tell us which it is, and we will correct the page.

It has been a protected natural monument since 2 May 1974, which puts it among the older designations on Freiburg's list. It stands on the corner of Einsteinstraße and Hermann-Mitsch-Straße in northern Freiburg, a separate outing from the old town rather than a stop on one.
